# Where Is the ISS?

The International Space Station circles the planet every ~92 minutes at 7.66 km/s, and [open-notify.org](http://open-notify.org) will tell you where it is right now — no key, CORS open, one GET:

```
GET http://api.open-notify.org/iss-now.json
→ {"iss_position": {"latitude": "-10.49", "longitude": "170.81"}, ...}
```

The JS cell takes one reading (falling back to a bundled fixture offline). The globe below then **polls live every 5 seconds**, accumulating the ground track. No map tiles are used (this app vendors everything, and the whole Earth won't fit in a notebook) — instead ten reference cities anchor your eyes. If the API is unreachable, the globe drives a simulated orbit at the ISS's real 51.6° inclination and says so.
Run the JS cell above, or wait - polling starts automatically.

## What the track teaches

Leave the globe running for ten minutes. The pink line is a **sine wave on a sphere**: the orbit is a fixed circle tilted 51.6° from the equator, but Earth rotates underneath it, so each successive pass crosses the equator ~22.9° further west. That westward crawl is why the ISS eventually flies over *every* point between 51.6°N and 51.6°S — and why it never visits Helsinki (60°N).

The JS cell is the honest API half: one request, explicit fixture fallback, no polling — the pattern for anything you'd run headless. The HTML cell is the live half: browser-resident polling with graceful degradation to a physics-based simulation.

## Try this

- Note the lat/lon, wait exactly 10 minutes, note it again — you should see ~39° of arc. Check against 360°/92.9 min.
- Add your home town to the `CITIES` list and watch for a flyover (|lat| must be under 51.6°… sorry, Reykjavik).
- Swap the API for astronauts: `http://api.open-notify.org/astros.json` lists everyone currently off-planet — render it as a caption.
- Compute and display the distance from the ISS ground point to the nearest reference city (haversine formula — 20 lines).
